package_info.package_versions: Affected versions as per CVE-2017-8046 (exact versions not specified in the report)
package_info.why_malicious: The package contains a critical vulnerability (CVE-2017-8046) that enables attackers to exploit insecure deserialization in the Spring Data REST framework. This flaw allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP PATCH requests containing malicious serialized objects, which are then deserialized without proper validation or type restriction, potentially resulting in remote code execution. While the vulnerability is unintentional, its presence allows for severe malicious exploitation.

execution_context.trigger: At HTTP request handling time (when a PATCH request is received)
execution_context.file_location: Java controller class in Spring Data REST handling PATCH requests (e.g., RepositoryRestController or similar)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At HTTP request handling time, the code deserializes attacker-supplied HTTP PATCH request bodies using a generic ObjectMapper, allowing untrusted data to be converted into arbitrary Java objects, which can result in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deserializing untrusted user input directly with a generic ObjectMapper is highly dangerous, as it allows attackers to supply serialized objects that may instantiate arbitrary classes or trigger malicious code paths during deserialization.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal secure behavior would restrict deserialization to a safe, whitelisted set of types and validate input before processing. The actual behavior allows arbitrary deserialization of user-supplied data, violating secure coding practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate deserialization occurs when data comes from trusted sources or is strictly validated and type-restricted, such as deserializing known DTOs from authenticated internal services.
key_indicators: Direct deserialization of @RequestBody data from HTTP PATCH requests
Use of ObjectMapper.readValue on untrusted input
Absence of type whitelisting or input validation in deserialization logic
Deserialization logic present in REST controller methods

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted HTTP PATCH request containing a malicious serialized Java object to the vulnerable REST endpoint.
attack_chain.leads_to: The application receives and processes attacker-controlled serialized data.

attack_chain.action: The vulnerable code deserializes the malicious payload using ObjectMapper, instantiating attacker-specified classes and potentially executing arbitrary code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential remote code execution or further exploitation within the application context.

behavioral_signatures: Deserialization of user-supplied data in HTTP PATCH request handlers
Use of ObjectMapper.readValue or similar deserialization APIs on @RequestBody parameters without type restriction
REST endpoints accepting arbitrary object types in PATCH/PUT/POST requests
file_indicators: Java controller classes annotated with @RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.PATCH)
Methods accepting @RequestBody Object or generic types
Presence of ObjectMapper.readValue or similar calls on HTTP request data
network_indicators: Unusual or malformed HTTP PATCH requests to REST endpoints
HTTP request bodies containing serialized Java object payloads (e.g., binary or suspiciously structured JSON)
Repeated PATCH requests from untrusted sources targeting RESTful endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Perform static analysis of REST controller code to identify deserialization of user-supplied data without type restrictions, especially in PATCH request handlers. Monitor network traffic for PATCH requests with serialized object payloads. Use runtime instrumentation to detect deserialization of unexpected or dangerous types during HTTP request processing. Flag endpoints that accept generic object types in request bodies and invoke ObjectMapper.readValue or similar APIs without input validation.
